posts.text:
Bitcoin mining software firm Luxor hacked: attackers steal 0.243 $BTC in rewards from miners

"In case you're wondering, what Luxor does is they make software that lets Bitcoin miners manage their machines. So it's not doing the mining, it's the software that does the management."

"Attackers were able to compromise that software, apparently using AI, and changed where the machines sent their mining work. So the miners kept paying for the electricity and doing the actual mining, but the attacker collected the Bitcoin rewards, which were sent to their wallet."

"It wasn't a huge amount, but again, another novel attack surface that nobody had seen coming for crypto-related software, and it becomes absolutely exhausting."

"So far this is only 0.243 Bitcoin. But if you're mining Bitcoin or looking at Bitcoin miners or using software that's related to it, now you have to be worried about that as well."

"The miners got the electricity bill for it, but the hacker got the direct deposit."

SemiAnalysis is cutting its AI infrastructure forecasts, with the biggest reductions coming in 2028–2030.

Three key drivers:
- Lower AI revenue expectations: Slowing net new ARR at frontier labs means compute supply additions need to become more sustainable.
- Tighter capital markets: Debt and equity investors are becoming less willing to finance AI capex, particularly projects without hyperscaler backing.
- Regulatory delays: US midterm-related uncertainty pushes out 5.8GW of planned datacenter capacity, with further regulatory delays affecting 2028.

$NVDA bears the brunt. Customers will increasingly prioritize performance per dollar and performance per watt, meaning weaker platforms face disproportionate spending cuts. MediaTek's TPU program is also exposed relative to $AVGO.

Importantly, the reduction in total spending is driven largely by lower pricing, alongside reduced unit volumes and lower HBM pricing assumptions.

The AI infrastructure buildout isn't stopping, but expectations are being reset. Competition, financing constraints and power availability are becoming increasingly important.

posts.name: CK Capital
posts.text:
The $NVDA guide tomorrow could cause a lot of uncertainty, and I do not think people are ready for it.

This is an interim CEO’s first print. Interim leadership almost never swings big on a guide, the playbook is conservative, guide wide, lower the bar you just inherited, leave room to beat later. Kress is a career CFO on top of it, careful is her default setting. Do not be surprised by a wider range than the tight band they have given for years, or less detail than usual.

The problem is this market cannot tell the difference between caution and confession right now. 

A conservative first guide is completely normal corporate behavior, but after the month $NVDA just had, a soft or wide number gets read as confirmation of every fear out there. That is how you get violent moves off a quarter that was actually fine.

Either way, expect uncertainty into and out of this one.

posts.name: Gad Nishimwe
posts.text:
$NVDA reports earnings tomorrow, and this could be one of its most important reports yet.

Look at NVIDIA's earnings history:

GAAP EPS:
• Aug 2024: $0.66
• Aug 2025: $1.08
• Aug 2026: $2.46

That's 128% earnings growth in just one year, with the latest quarter setting a new high in our 12-report study.

What Wall Street expects tomorrow:
- Revenue: ~$109B
- Adjusted EPS: ~$2.47
- NVIDIA's own revenue guidance: ~$108B

But this earnings report is different.

Jensen Huang has stepped down, and interim CEO Colette Kress faces her first major test. Investors will be watching AI demand, profit margins, future guidance, and leadership plans.

My biggest question: With earnings growing this fast but the stock down more than 30% from its October peak, will another strong quarter be enough to restore investor confidence?
$NVDA @tastyliveshow #NVDA

posts.text: Uhhh what is semianalysis doing…?

quoted.text:
〈下調加速器需求與出貨量展望；NVIDIA 承受重壓〉

1、下修幅度 1）SemiAnalysis 在機構版內容中下調了未來 AI 晶片出貨量、相關支出和用電需求的預測，2028年起的調整最明顯，NVIDIA（ $NVDA）是受影響最大的供應商。 2）2028年全球 AI 加速器資本支出預測從約1.05兆美元降到7,580億美元，下調28%。 3）2030年預測從約1.53兆美元降到9,230億美元，下調40%。 4）報告截圖說明，下修原因包括出貨量下降、價格下降，以及調整了2029和2030年未來加速器的單晶片功耗假設。

2、下修的三大原因 1）重新設定生態系的總 Token 收入預期：Frontier Labs 第三季淨新增 ARR（年度經常性收入）成長放緩，所以下調新增供給的預估，讓收入能持續覆蓋整體算力成本。SemiAnalysis 說自己對實驗室收入的預期仍比市場共識樂觀，也看到很多值得部署前沿智慧、投資報酬率高的領域，但資本市場參與者的平均預期對基礎建設融資非常關鍵。 2）資本市場收緊：債權和股權投資人都不願投資 AI 建置相關的資本支出，沒有超大規模雲端業者承租的案子尤其如此。這會減少資料中心用地、電力和廠殼開發，可供部署系統的電力供給因此下降。 3）美國期中選舉結果：原本規劃在2027年下半年到2028年上半年建置的5.8GW 美國資料中心供給被延後，監管延遲也在減少2028年的資料中心總容量。SemiAnalysis 說這確實讓近期算力設備出貨量下降，但前兩項因素更重要。

3、衝擊不平均：NVIDIA 首當其衝 1）SemiAnalysis 的架構是，客戶會優先選擇效能、TCO（總擁有成本）和每瓦效能最好的晶片，再疊加融資支援；在這些指標上排名最差的平台和晶片，會被不成比例地削減。 2）結果是 NVIDIA 受影響最大，承擔了大部分的支出削減。 3）ASIC 方面，聯發科（MediaTek, http://2454.TW）的 TPU 項目也受影響，因為融資能力比 Broadcom（ $AVGO）弱。

posts.name: Gene Munster
posts.text:
What would happen to $NVDA earnings multiple if investors could sleep well?

We can learn a little bit by looking at what’s happened with $AAPL’s multiple over the past 15 years. Setting aside all of the near-term transition risk. 

During the iPhone’s hypergrowth phase from 2009 to 2011, AAPL’s earnings multiple expanded dramatically. But as growth began to slow, investors believed those hypergrowth days were behind it and the most attractive part of the story was over. As a result, AAPL’s multiple compressed to roughly 12x forward earnings in 2012.

What investors missed was that hardware can become a business with annuity characteristics if a company maintains a sustainable edge. Despite a brutal smartphone market, Apple showed it could maintain pricing power, retain customers, and generate recurring revenue through predictable hardware upgrades.

Eventually, investors realized Apple didn’t need iPhone growth above 20% to be exceptional. Steady sleep well at night revenue growth of 5 to 10% and earnings growth of 10 to 15% proved hugely valuable, helping the multiple climb from roughly 12 times in 2012 to about 34x calendar 2027 earnings today.

Back to NVDA. The question isn’t just how long the current boom lasts, but whether the company can prove durable pricing power and a recurring upgrade cycle for its GPUs.

Those massive data centers being built today will need upgrading starting  in five years. If Nvidia keeps its edge and captures those upgrades, even with 10 to 15% earnings growth, you can make a case for a higher multiple.

The lesson from Apple is that valuation multiples don’t always peak when growth does. Sometimes the biggest expansion comes when investors can sleep well at night given durability and predictability become clear.

The big question: can the market's powerful V-shaped rebound develop into a sustainable recovery, or is another selloff coming?

*

So, $SPY V-bottom or W-bottom?

After $SPY declined roughly 6% toward $732, I deployed 25% of my Blood in the Street Account into long-term positions. 

The subsequent snapback created excellent trading opportunities, but the rally has now encountered resistance around $763, another lower high near the previous breakdown.

The critical levels are $753 and Friday's $747 low. If buyers defend these areas, the market could establish a constructive W-shaped bottom before attempting another move higher. 

A breakdown, however, would raise the possibility of retesting the lows.

With very few constructive stock setups and limited leadership, I remain cautious about the sustainability of the rebound.

*

$NVDA earnings this week could be a major rurning point.

Nvidia has suffered a nearly 40% correction from approximately $240 to $148, where a hammer-like reversal and strong volume triggered a sharp rebound.

I see $158, Friday's low, as the immediate level to watch. 

Holding it could create another tactical opportunity, potentially even a red-to-green reversal. Losing it would weaken the setup.

While Nvidia may meet or beat earnings expectations and deliver strong guidance, I believe significant overhead resistance and uncertainty surrounding Jensen Huang could limit the upside.

Unlike previous 40%+ corrections that recovered within months, I doubt Nvidia will reclaim its former highs anytime soon. 

A post-earnings bounce may be tradable, but that doesn't necessarily mean the longer-term damage has been repaired.

*

ANTHROPIC IPO: THE "ART OF THE FIRST DAY" $ANT

I discussed so many times how I approach major IPOs using a strategy developed over two decades.

Rather than chasing hype, I watch the opening print, the first five-minute candle, and the initial trading range. 

If buyers establish control and the stock breaks above its opening range, opportunities can emerge. If it cannot even reclaim its opening price, I prefer to stay away.

$SPCX and $CRBS were a great recent examples.

*

The speculation that #SpaceX could acquire #Tesla before Christmas is growing, potentially streamlining Elon Musk's businesses. 

$420 is a hypothetical transaction price but nothing is confirmed yet, so take this with the grain of sault.

Technically, $385 is the immediate level to defend. Holding it would demonstrate impressive relative strength, while a breakdown could bring $370 into focus.

I would even consider some $TSLL exposure in case the rumored transaction materializes.

*

Bottom line: this week could determine whether the market's recovery gains credibility or turns into another selling opportunity. 

Watch the levels above, respect the risks, and remember: a powerful snapback is not the same as a repaired market!

posts.name: Revere Asset Management
posts.text:
📺 What You Need To Know Ahead Of This Week: $NVDA Earnings, $ANT Anthropic’s IPO, & A Fragile Stock Market

Please ❤️like and 🔁share with fellow growth stock investors

@toddmichael70 provides an update ahead of the new week, noting that the market remains in a fragile position heading into a potentially pivotal week, with #Nvidia earnings, Anthropic's IPO in focus, rising Treasury yields, and a compromised $QQQ follow-through day raising serious questions about the sustainability of the recent rebound.

*

We still classify the market as Neutral, but leadership remains in "Protect mode". 

The November 11 Nasdaq follow-through day initially offered hope for a recovery, yet very few stocks were breaking out of sound bases. 

$QQQ has since closed twice below the follow-through-day low, casting doubt on the strength of the signal.

*

Technically, the picture remains mixed:

$QQQ and the S&P 500 are trading below their 21-day and 50-day moving averages, while equal-weight $RSP remains above both. 

Longer term, $QQQ is hovering just below its 200-day, the S&P 500 $SPX / $SPY and $RSP remain above theirs, and the Russell 2000 $IWM is below.

This divergence highlights an important shift: money is rotating away from battered mega-cap technology stocks into more defensive areas and companies holding up after earnings.

*

Our Revere AI 100 index surged 7.82% last week, helping fuel the Nasdaq's rebound. 

But after multiple weeks of heavy selling, much of that strength appears to be an oversold bounce rather than a sustainable recovery. 

Very few AI stocks are forming proper bases.

*

Meanwhile, market breadth remains troubling. 

Net new lows continue climbing, and the S&P 500 is struggling beneath a declining 50-day moving average. 

Although formal distribution has yet to emerge, the underlying market environment remains unhealthy.

*

$NVDA is another major wildcard. 

Following Jensen Huang's removal as CEO and allegations involving Chinese espionage, questions are emerging about whether the decision was rushed and whether the accusations have merit. These claims remain unverified.

With #NVDA earnings approaching, investors will be watching closely. 

But even strong results may struggle to restore confidence amid leadership uncertainty and broader technology-sector weakness.

*

On the macro front, hot CPI and PPI readings have pushed Treasury yields sharply higher last week.

There is a near-certain expectation for a 25-basis-point Fed rate hike, with one governor reportedly advocating 50 basis points. 

Higher borrowing costs and rising yields remain significant headwinds for growth stocks.

*

This week's calendar also includes $HD earnings, retail sales, industrial production, capacity utilization, new home sales, and FOMC minutes.

*

Another major event on everyone's radar is Anthropic's anticipated IPO, which could become a significant catalyst for the AI sector. 

As investors increasingly question the sustainability of massive AI capital expenditures, circular financing arrangements, and stretched technology valuations, Anthropic's public-market debut could provide an important test of investor appetite for AI-related investments. 

Strong demand could help revive enthusiasm across the sector, while a disappointing reception could reinforce concerns about an increasingly fragile AI investment boom.

*

The bottom line: the November 11 follow-through day remains compromised, market leadership is scarce, and rising new lows suggest selling pressure hasn't disappeared.

Until the major indexes reclaim key moving averages and stronger leadership emerges, the recent rebound deserves caution rather than conviction.

*

Watch this Short video where @toddmichael70 breaks it all down in detail 🔽

If I were a well-connected investor with a massive position in $NVDA and wanted to unload it, here's what I could do:

I'd call one or two equally well-connected investors. Together, we'd get Jensen on the phone and ask him something like:

"What would have to happen for you to come back?"

Even if Jensen replied, "There's absolutely nothing on this planet that could convince me to return," I'd find a way to reframe that conversation into a story retail investors would love to hear.

Then I'd feed it to a media outlet hungry for a market-moving headline.

The next morning, as retail investors rushed in on renewed hope, I'd open the floodgates and unload my position into their buying.

Exit liquidity secured. Mission accomplished.

Of course, this is purely hypothetical. But it illustrates just how easily a conversation can be turned into a narrative that serves someone else's financial interests.

posts.text:
𝗦𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗔𝗻𝗮𝗹𝘆𝘀𝗶𝘀 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗰𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝘀 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘅 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗮𝘀𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗡𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘁 $NVDA

In its Nov 13th institutional model update, SemiAnalysis lowered its forecasts for AI accelerator shipments, spending, HBM and power demand, with 2028 to 2030 cut the hardest.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿𝘀 (𝗴𝗹𝗼𝗯𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘅)

• 2026: ~$392B, roughly unchanged
• 2027: $770B to $627B (-19%)
• 2028: $1.054T to $758B (-28%)
• 2029: $1.352T to $796B (-41%)
• 2030: $1.531T to $923B (-40%)

Also cut: 2028 HBM demand by 30% and 2030 accelerator power demand by 34%.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗰𝘂𝘁

• Frontier lab net new ARR growth slowed in Q3, so they reset expected token revenue to what can sustainably pay for compute
• Capital markets have tightened. Debt and equity investors are pulling back from AI capex that lacks hyperscaler commitments
• The midterm results delayed 5.8 GW of US data center supply planned for 2H27 to 1H28, though they stress the first two reasons matter more

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗡𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗶𝗮 𝗯𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘁

The cuts don't land evenly. Customers keep buying the best performance per TCO and per watt, and the weakest platforms on those metrics take disproportionate cuts. By their framework, that is Nvidia:
• Nvidia accounts for 66% of the cut in cumulative 2026 to 2030 accelerator wafer area
• Its 2030 shipment forecast on a compute revenue basis is cut 66%
• Lower ASP assumptions for Feynman and beyond as competition rises
• At Anthropic, Nvidia GPUs sit at the margin next to TPU, Trainium and AMD. OpenAI is leaning on AMD and its own ASICs
• Highest exposure to neoclouds, especially the smaller long tail with more financing risk

𝗠𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲

Read this carefully. It is not a call that AI demand is dying. Even on the new numbers, accelerator capex more than doubles from $392B in 2026 to $923B in 2030.

What it says is that the buildout is now limited by financing and revenue, not chips. That ties directly to what I have been saying about liquidity and the Anthropic raise pulling capital out of the market.

The winners from here are whoever has the best cost per token and the strongest balance sheet behind the order. Coming the same week Jensen left and the Treasury Secretary questioned Nvidia's revenue quality, this is one more weight on Tuesday's guide.

Translated excerpt attached. Credit @dmjk001 for original excerpt.

StockTwits community has turned unusually bearish on AI stocks after the recent selloff, with a rare flood of negative commentary on valuations, debt, and the build-out. The mix of widespread retail bearishness and high short interest creates classic short-squeeze conditions. Mega-caps remain less heavily shorted, and risks persist, but the positioning is there for a sharp reversal.

My first $100k meant more to me than my first $1,000,000.

Let me explain.

I started with about $6,000 in college. 16 years and 20,000+ trades later, I’ve lost $800k. I’ve lost another $500k averaging down on SPX. I’ve lost almost $2M in a silver flash crash.

But what kept me in the game was the skill I’d built.

A lot of young traders are chasing getting funded and chasing a payout right now. Pass the evaluation, get paid, run it back.

If that’s the whole plan, you’re learning how to get funded and nothing else. When the funding goes away, you’ve got nothing to stand on.

Prop firms can be a way in. Just don’t make it your home. Use it to learn risk, build a record, and work toward trading on your own.

Always prioritize building the actual skill.

Re: The new BIS rule

I missed a provision yesterday.

Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the existing transistor-count verification process unless they have BIS status as an “approved” or “authorized” IC designer. Under the previous rule, a foundry or an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider could verify the transistor count to establish eligibility for an exemption. Now, BIS itself has to decide whether to grant one.

As a result, foundries such as TSMC and Samsung Electronics, as well as OSAT providers such as ASE and Amkor, will need to conduct more thorough background checks on their customers.

CHASE SAYS THE OUTAGE WAS ITS OWN HARDWARE, NOT AN ATTACK

JPMorgan Chase said the disruption that hit its online banking and some branches today came from a software bug in on-premise hardware systems, and that it was not cyber related.

The bank said customers kept access to their accounts and funds throughout, that some were taking longer than usual to serve, and that it expected service back by the end of the day.

It also addressed the spread to other lenders. Other banks were affected only where they were a party to a transaction with Chase, the bank said. That matters, because reports through the afternoon named several banks with problems and complaints spiked at more than one on outage trackers.

The timing invited a different explanation. Microsoft 365 and Outlook went down earlier the same afternoon, and the two were widely connected as the day went on. Chase's account does not support that link. It points at its own equipment, on its own premises.

No post-incident report has been published, so what the bug actually did is still the bank's description and nothing more.

Source: JPMorgan Chase statement, 16 November

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Don’t Hike Into a Mirage: Wall Street’s March Rate Rise Would Land on a Energy Glut

Wall Street wants the Fed to hike into March. The energy glut and the base effects say that would be a mistake.

The glut is already showing up at the pump. Wholesale gasoline futures for December delivery closed at $2.53 a gallon today, down 18.4% in four weeks and 20% from the late-October high of $3.18. Today alone they fell 3.4%, to a fresh one-month low. 

This is the physical market confirming what the IEA already reported: supply above demand for the first time since the Iran war began, inventories up 52m barrels in October, and Brent 30% off its peak. Retail prices follow wholesale with a lag of a few weeks.

Headline CPI is about to look hot for the wrong reason. Even with pump prices flat, inflation climbs from 3.7% to about 4.1% by January, only because it’s measured against last winter’s cheap gasoline. That’s arithmetic, not new inflation. Excluding gasoline, inflation is already running at 2.8%.

Then the math flips. In March, the spring 2026 war spike drops out of the comparison, and headline falls by about three-quarters of a point in a single month. 

With wholesale already down 20%, our steepest scenario is now the one playing out, and it takes headline inflation to about 1.7% by May, below the Fed’s target.

So the Street is asking the Fed to tighten at the peak of a statistical illusion, into a gasoline market already in free fall. Hiking into March means tightening into the steepest drop in headline inflation of the cycle. That isn’t prudence. It’s driving by the rear-view mirror.

The Fed shouldn’t take its cue from Wall Street’s fear of a January print. It should look through it.

posts.text:
What I’m currently building with AI: self-improving Read-through system

This is entirely focused on the Consumer sector – currently at a 55% hit rate (your read-through to ANT = positive – this will need the frontier for a long long time)

Every week, the system goes through the docs hitting our system and puts them through a funnel. From the initial docs, the relevant statements within them expand the set of impacted categories ~4x (ie a TGT probably opines on a handful of end markets being strong or weak).

From that 4x expansion, there’s a screen of what qualifies as a credible read – which brings it back to ~1x.

The system then leverages the very intricate supply chain mapping AlphaSense built to expand the list of companies impacted by the read roughly another 4x based on each category flowing through the criteria of a credible read.

We then run validation layers to make sure the company relationship passes through based on the specific comment (ie was there trade-down, eat at home vs. away, do the product lines overlap, etc) – getting us back down ~0.3x calls, with a strength of signal score.

Every week, it runs an eval of the results. Early on, a good chunk of them were just errors – you could have a share shift that hurts the target company but the initial read would have said positive because of a company level relationship. True logic errors are becoming less common (though that does not mean it got a stock movement right – that’s a much higher bar).

It builds ideas based on US Consumer companies >$3bn mkt cap, trading a full day after the read (not gaming the pre-market) – through the next 42 days (what the system determined to be covering the gap from read-through through target earnings. Not pressure tested)

Read-throughs → Sector supply chain map / relationships → Evals → Self-improvement

Within this, there is one particular strategy that is printing $$ – which is positive read-throughs on beaten down (>10% down) stocks. This part is hindsight though.

Do I expect this Sharpe to continue from just this – probably not.

Where I’m going next is chaining together my pieces:
Read-through system
Channel Check correlation system
Forecasting system which uses prior two as inputs 
IC Memo System which uses forecasts and builds valuation analysis through r/r

The concept is that this goes to manual fundamental Hedge Fund depth, but at quantitative scale.

Any quants interested in collaborating, lmk.

posts.text:
What was the significance of this weekend's SpaceX tower catch: 

"Catching the second stage is substantially harder than catching the first stage because the Ship returns from orbit while the booster returns from a short suborbital hop. The booster separates minutes after liftoff, performs a brief boostback, and comes back from only a few hundred kilometers away at relatively low speed. Ship must reach orbital velocity, deploy payload, coast for many hours, execute a precise deorbit burn, survive full reentry heating, and only then perform its landing burn. As such, Ship must carry a functional heat shield, fly a long guided atmospheric trajectory from the other side of the planet, and execute a high-energy flip into the “chopsticks” while protecting its heat-shield side. Those combined demands of orbital energy, thermal protection, long-range guidance, and final precision are why a Ship catch is so incredibly difficult. No prior system, including the Space Shuttle, recovered a rocket-style orbital stage in this manner. The catch validates the path to full reusability which is the foundation of Starship’s cost and cadence targets. This is particularly important in driving the economics of orbital data centers." - DB

AI and 24-Hour Trading Test Rules Governing Currency Markets

The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and round-the-clock trading is raising questions about whether rules governing the $9.5 trillion foreign-exchange market can keep pace with technological change.

The FX Global Code, a set of voluntary standards for conduct in currency markets, may need more frequent reviews to keep pace with advances in AI, according to Manuel Mondedeu, co-head of global foreign exchange at CIBC Capital Markets and co-vice chair of the Global Foreign Exchange Committee. The goal is to make implementation “a bit more dynamic” without changing the underlying principles, he said Monday at a Federal Reserve Bank of New York conference.

The move toward 24-hour trading and instant settlement using blockchain and tokenization could create additional challenges, Nordstrom said. Those include thinner liquidity, fewer opportunities to offset transactions and greater volatility during quieter trading periods. (Bloomberg)

We just raised $53M from Accel India, Together Fund, and Premji Invest to build the CRM that Salesforce should have been.

Every legacy CRM works the same way: you do the actual work all day, then you do it all over again by typing it into the CRM.

Brad Gerstner says the Nvidia board answers to shareholders, not Congress, and should take its time on Jensen Huang

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Rate rises do not cool services inflation!

Services inflation has spent 94.6 per cent of the past 58 years above 2 per cent. Its long-run average is 4.76 per cent. The latest reading, for September, stands at 3.2 per cent. The historical record is clear: aggressive monetary tightening does not reliably or quickly return services inflation to target.

The series in question is the CPI for services less energy, a proxy for the sticky component of the price level. It has fallen below 2 per cent in only three episodes. The first was the 1983 Volcker recession, which was flattered by a change in how housing costs were measured. The second was the aftermath of the global financial crisis, and the third was the pandemic. Each time it took a collapse in demand, not a rate path. The recent hiking cycle has left it at 3.2 per cent, well above the Federal Reserve’s goal.

Alan Blinder’s 1982 analysis of the 1970s inflation episode remains instructive. He separated special factors, such as food and energy shocks and the end of price controls, from the baseline or underlying rate driven by longer-run forces. 

The former can reverse once the shocks fade; the latter moves slowly. Extend his framework to today and services, with their contractual and administered prices, sit firmly in the baseline category. Tight policy can cool flexible goods prices and restrain demand. It has far less near-term traction on sticky service prices.

Policymakers who treat services inflation as a demand problem open to rapid correction therefore risk over-tightening. The costs appear in output and employment; the benefits to the services component arrive late, if at all. 

The six-decade chart is not an argument against any policy response to inflation. It is an argument against the belief that rate rises are a reliable instrument for bringing services inflation to 2 per cent on a politically convenient timetable.

posts.name: Daniel Newman
posts.text:
Today's forecast revision from SemiAnalysis is pretty interesting. 

The TLDR is it calls for a 28% cut in AI accelerator capex in 2028 and then 41% and 40% cut the following two years respectively. 

The composition of these cuts was about 17% on shipments, and it has NVIDIA taking the brunt (66%) of the cut. 

Basically, demand in the past 10 days has been completely nuked? Remember, it was on election day that SA published this reiterating just how fast the build out is going. 

“We wrote at length about how SpaceX’s plans for 10GW in 2027 was feasible, paving the way for +300b+ ARR. We received a lot of pushback from folks calling it impossible. Now, just two months later, we’re already seeing 3.6GW under construction across multiple sites, both existing and new. SpaceX has even revised its estimate up to ~13GW in 2027. This would be the largest amount of datacenter capacity ever built by any one company in that timeframe, roughly equivalent to all of Google’s datacenter capacity from 1999-2026 in just 1.5 years. We think it’s possible and have already identified >9GW of capacity.”

The forecast cut doesn't mention or reflect anything related to China exports or API use. But it does call for a significant slowdown in the growth of the frontier labs. This is also interesting in both the narrative and the timing given the Anthropic IPO this week.

The report as interpreted indicates that HBM pricing will see double digit % price declines and ASPs on Feynman SKUs would take a 40% haircut from estimates with Feynman dropping from $110k  b78k and estimates on Feynman Next dropping from $191k to $118k. 

A lot has to happen for demand to slow this much and for the semiconductor supply chain to normalize this much in a short period of time. 

While the report claims that its revision is based on 3 factors. 

1. Lab monetization slow down. 
2. Stricter access to to capital
3. Election-based data center delays. 

The revision is much harsher than a handful of GW being slowed by red tape. 

The report basically insinuates that the demand asymmetry is drying up in 2027. That in-house silicon projects are taking off at a dramatic pace, but only so much so that the memory wall will have been climbed. 
66% of the revision down comes from NVIDIA. But again, why would its margins suffer so badly? 
In reality we have a lab IPO with $900 Billion in compute commits. 

We have uncertain demand in China, but no matter how much exports are restricted or tightened, it is hard to believe it will just stop seeking compute. And don't tell me NVIDIA demand will be replaced by Huawei Ascend. (It won't)

It almost feels like SA is saying without saying that China is a MUCH BIGGER consumer of NVIDIA chips? And without it and its labs chewing up Inference on Anthropic and OpenAI and it using "NVIDIA" to train its models that the domestic demand will faulter substantially. If China really was utilizing a disproportionate amount of compute at peak prices this could cause a major downturn in margins for NVIDIA. 

Our forecasts (@ETRnews and @TheFuturumGroup) see much more modest scenarios with some newly minted downside risk. We agree that 27 is locked in and we see the same for most of 28. Projects into 29 and beyond have time for negotiation, but the compute demand for inference and agents will continue to climb dramatically. Some GW could slip and elongate the cycle. But seeing ASPs drop 40% on roughly the same volume suggests a structural weakening and a supply chain overcorrection or an underlying symptom that simply isn't reflected in lab demand, financing, or election outcomes. Perhaps China holds the key?

posts.name: Sam Kovacs
posts.text:
THE LAST STAGE OF THE BUBBLE LOOKS LIKE THIS:  

1. The S&P 500 is only 3% below its October 6 record. If you only looked at the index, you'd think nothing has really happened.   

2. But that would be wrong. The top 20 tech stocks, which make up 40% of the S&P 500, are down 9.8% since the peak. The top 30 non-ten stocks are up 9.4%. The index is holding up because money is rotating out of tech. But this does not make a healthy market. (Chart 1)  

3. Leaders lead. In every bull market, the leaders turn first, and the index lags. Jesse Livermore wrote about this in 1923. He remarked that a market stops being a bull market before the whole index breaks, and the tail is when the leaders fall one after another and, "for the first time in months do not come back."  

4. This is already happening. 80% of the 50 biggest winners of this bull market are now in a bear market (20% below their peak). The last time it was this high, in April 2025, the index had already fallen by 19%. Today it is only down 3% (chart 2).   

5. We first saw the most speculative names unwind. Now the stocks which have added the most market cap in this bull market are unwinding too. The biggest of them all, Nvidia, is 32% below its record, while the index sits very close to its high (chart 3).   

6. The final piece of the puzzle is what Jerry Grantham noted in his studies. In both 1929 and 2000, the speculative stocks had fallen about 30% before the market broke, while a shrinking group of blue chips kept rising.   

7. That's exactly what we're seeing today. Of the top 50. gainers, 23 of them peaked early in the summer. They are down 31% since then as a group while the 10 largest non tech blue chips are up 25%. These moves have sped up since the October 6th peak (Chart 4)  

8. This is mostly flows. Money leaving tech into blue chip. As long as this leg lasts there. is money to be made on both the long and the short. When the blue chip rally ends, either it was a temporary pullback or it all falls down.

posts.name: Chris McGuire
posts.text:
NEW: The Department of Commerce just published new AI and semiconductor export control regulations that close some major loopholes in existing export controls. The regulation includes new rules to: (1) counter Chinese smuggling of AI chips; (2) restrict Chinese companies from renting access to AI chips; and (3) block Chinese chip designers from making AI chips at TSMC.

These rules are a major step forward. They still contain some key gaps that need to be filled urgently in a follow-up rule, namely, they do not block Chinese companies from buying AI chips inside the United States or renting access to AI chips at US-based data centers. However, this rule will help and is the first good-faith effort to actually close loopholes in export controls in a year and a half. Hopefully more will follow.

1.  Countering Chinese smuggling of AI chips. The rule expands export controls on AI chips to five new countries: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. It does not block AI chip orders to these countries, but requires a US government review (unless it is a US company that meets certain requirements). This is a massively needed step. Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia have been the second, fourth, fifth, and eighth biggest importers of AI chips this year. 

The rule doesn’t cover Taiwan itself, where chip smuggling is a massive issue (exports of AI chips to China are still not illegal under Taiwanese law), and still doesn’t prevent AI chip sales to Chinese companies in the United States, which somehow remain legal. Ultimately, large orders of AI chips by untrusted companies in any country should require a license to fully combat smuggling, as Chinese companies will move to buy AI chips anywhere there isn’t a license requirement. But this is a start.

2.  Restricting Chinese companies from renting access to AI chips. The rule creates a new remote access control that restricts companies from providing Chinese companies with remote access to AI chips. It requires a US export license to provide Chinese companies with access to 12 million TPP or more (equivalent to ~200 of the most advanced Blackwell chips, or ~800 H100 chips). This applies to chips already shipped, as well as all future shipments. Some of these requirements even apply retroactively; Commerce says existing rules already barred data supplying a majority of a data center’s compute to Chinese companies, and tells companies that violated this to self-disclose. This effectively kills the business of neoclouds like Megaspeed that exist to provide remote access to large amounts of AI compute to China. 

The biggest gap is the remote access controls do not apply to data centers in the United States. So Chinese companies can legally train on large numbers of Blackwells at data centers in Northern Virginia. This gap should be closed immediately with a new rule that uses Commerce’s US persons authority to capture this activity. The rule also exempts recommendation algorithms, so impact will depend on enforcement. Last, new authorities included in the text of the AI Overwatch Act would strengthen Commerce's ability to enforce these controls--that bill should pass immediately. 

3.  Blocking Chinese chip designers from making AI chips at TSMC. The rule closes loopholes in existing controls that Chinese companies are likely exploiting to illicitly make AI chips at TSMC or Samsung. Specifically, it now requires any Chinese chip designer who is seeking to make a 16/14nm or more advanced chip at TSMC/Samsung to get a U.S. export license, and restores old rules that weren’t being enforced until now that require any untrusted company anywhere in the world to get a license to make an AI chip at TSMC or Samsung. This is a significant upgrade.

Overall, this is a major step forward to countering Chinese smuggling of and access to advanced AI chips. The work here is not done, as there are some critical loopholes that remain open and need to be closed in a follow-up rule (na

Canada’s CPI is about to lie to you.

Gas prices fell 2.5% last month, but gasoline inflation rose to 30.9%. Why? Base effects. Last October’s price drop fell out of the math.

Expect “inflation is back” headlines over the holidays. It’s arithmetic, not a trend.

Watch and prepare for the BOC act irresponsibly. 

Then comes March. The war spike drops out of the base, gasoline y/y falls 20–35 points in two months, and headline lands between 1.5% and 2.2%.

The disinflation is already baked in. The only question is whether central banks see it, or tighten on last winter’s gas prices.

Don’t panic. Ask why.

posts.text:
What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part? A rare podcast focused on everything around building software, with @satyanadella.  Timestamps:

00:00 Intro
02:12 Microsoft’s open-source shift
04:15 Building VS Code in the open
05:55 Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code
09:52 Decision engines
12:32 Verifying AI-generated code
15:39 The software factory
20:45 Bringing AI to existing products
24:06 Why adopting AI is different to adopting React
26:29 The changing role of software engineers
29:25 Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers
34:05 AI anxiety and changing roles
36:35 Junior hiring
42:36 Open models
45:39 Owning your AI infrastructure
51:21 Building trust in AI agents
53:48 Local models and hybrid intelligence
56:39 Microsoft’s model strategy
59:26 Advice for engineers
1:01:21 Closing takeaways

Brought to you by:

• @turbopuffer  – a vector and full-text search engine built on object storage. It’s fast, cheap, and extremely scalable. https://turbopuffer.com/pragmatic (I built a greatly improved podcast/newseltter search with it, check it out: http://pragmaticengineer.com/search)

• @linear  – the product development system for teams and agents. https://linear.app/pragmatic

• @WorkOS  – everything you need to make your app enterprise-ready. https://workos.com/

3 interesting takeaways from Satya:

1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. 

Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work.

2. “Own the intelligence”: avoid lock-in & treat agents as an insider risk. 

Satya cautions companies to avoid lock-in with any single model provider by ensuring that the harness, memory, and model are not coupled, so that they can be changed with ease. He also thinks more companies should consider using open models as a way to protect their core intellectual property (IP) from leaking out, and build private evals to decide what models to use and upgrade to. He also says that models are intelligent but unreliable, so it’s best to treat them as “insider risks” and build a separate system to verify that agentic systems work as expected.

3. What’s with those voluntary exit offers? 

I asked Satya directly why Microsoft recently made voluntary exit offers to most of its software engineers for the first time in the company’s history. I also wanted to know if it could mean layoffs in the future. Unsurprisingly, his reply was diplomatic, but in the podcast I rehashed what I heard in a more direct way.

http://Northstarbadcharts.com website article for members dated Jan 12th 2026 (2 weeks before gold & silver topped out)...

First things first – are you a longer term investor or stacker? If so, as always, just follow the signals in the TNS and DPM to ride the bull market trend.

If you have some shorter term strategies or if you’re trading, you’ll want to know when the shorter term charts break down, signalling an increased likelihood of a longer, deeper correction. Here’s golds daily chart… (SEE FIRST CHART)

We had a close call at the red arrow, but horizintal support held, and the uptrend continues. As long as we’re above those two rising red lines, there are no concerns.

I’ve been tracking silver on its 4-hour chart. Last week I wondered whether we could be seeing a topping pattern forming. It would’ve been confirmed if we broke through the lower support line near $72.50…that did not happen. Instead, we have an upside breakout and we continue upwards…(SEE SECOND CHART)

Looking at the long-term roadmap, gold may extend to the next Fib extension level to complete this move near $5300. In any case, you can see its distance from moving average indicator is now at a 1970’s level of ‘stretchedness’. This move is as historically important as the one 50+ years ago (SEE THIRD CHART)

It’s much the same for silver on its long-term chart…(SEE FOURTH CHART)

Fibonacci levels suggest a move above the $84 area might lead to the $128 area acting as a magnet. Wherever this move terminates, I would be surprised if we don’t fall more than 30%. A 50% drop wouldn’t surprise me. It also wouldn’t surprise me if the next major correction (whenever it comes) lasts for a year or more.

The prospect of a long and deep correction DOES NOT mean we’re bearish yet. It DOES NOT mean sell it all now. It also DOES NOT mean this bull market is over. Until the small timeframe charts break down there’s no evidence of a developing deeper corection. Sadly, with these metrics, there is no low risk entry point (that was back when the TNS gave its buy signals for gold and silver).

If you have a long-term strategy, that doesn’t necessarily mean you can’t enter the market, it just means that doing so in stages over a longer period of time may be wise, because that deeper correction can start anytime. As long as you’re aware of that, and prepered to weather that storm, for the much longer term bullish prospects, it’s ok.

There are other charts that are very close to giving low risk trade entry signals on the next monthly close though, and we’ll let you know if/when that happens.

posts.name: jeroen blokland
posts.text:
The euro just dropped to 1.10 against the US dollar.

The last time we saw the euro at this level was in April 2025.

Is this all the result of markets pricing in more rate hikes, and potentially a 50-basis-point move in December, from the Federal Reserve?

Well, interest rate differentials do explain part of the moves in fiat currency pairs.

But in the case of the Eurozone there is more: structural weakness.

Even though the Eurozone consists of a patchwork of very different countries, (monetary) policy must target the weakest link.

Currently the weakest link is France. France’s growth potential is low, its debt is high, and its social welfare system is out of control expensive. As a result, France’s bond spread is now at the levels seen during the height of the Eurozone debt crisis.

At some point another Eurozone debt crisis will emerge. And because (monetary) policy must always target the weakest link, it’s reasonable to assume the euro will weaken over time.

Against the US dollar, this is only partly visible, as the United States has quite a few (monetary) flaws too.

But measured against something outside the flawed (monetary) system, the structural weakness becomes impossible to deny.

Since the start of this century, the euro has depreciated a whopping 92% against gold. That is a lot. No wonder everything is so expensive. No wonder purchasing power is being destroyed on a massive scale.

What I am trying to point out is that chasing fiat currency pairs often does not tell you the whole story. We get paid, spend, save, and invest in a currency that is continuously being devalued. No doom-and-gloom story, just the facts.

And once you embrace the facts, doesn’t it make sense to try to avoid at least some of that continuous devaluation?

Charlie Shrem says crypto was years ahead of TradFi: Bitcoin had instant payments in 2011, when banks took 6 weeks to set up a transfer

"We had a fintech business with BitInstant. We had an account with every single bank, so I'm acutely aware of what their websites and back ends look like. Bank of America, PNC Bank, JPMorgan, Citibank. Zero software back then."

"You logged in in 2011, and it looked like it was a '90s website. That would take like 6 weeks of explaining to them why you want to be able to send money from your account to someone else's account."

"Bitcoin gave us that, the idea of instantly sending money from one person to another. In 2011, we had MPEx. Go look it up. It was the first ever way to sell shares of your company and receive Bitcoin, and Erik Voorhees IPO'd Satoshi Dice on it. We had real infrastructure of decentralized money plumbing."

"Nowadays, the Fed does same-day bank transfers, and whether you use Mercury or your bank, it looks like what a Bitcoin wallet looked like 6 years ago. Every bank looks like Coinbase, but Coinbase did it first."

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
The employment index improved primarily because fewer firms were cutting workers, not because hiring suddenly accelerated. Only 21.5% reported adding employees, while 75.1% reported no change. Meanwhile, new orders collapsed from 23.2 to just 3.0, with firms reporting rising orders plunging from 42.9% to 28.3%. 

Now examine the historical chart. Notice how previous peaks in manufacturing employment and hours were followed by sharp reversals, particularly around economic downturns. That happens because employment typically lags demand. Manufacturers maintain staffing to fulfill existing orders until weakening demand forces them to reduce hours and eventually headcount. 

Not every peak signals a recession, but celebrating employment strength while ignoring collapsing orders completely misses the possibility that today’s strongest labor readings are tomorrow’s lagging indicators of economic deterioration.

quoted.text: Employment was an area of strength in today's New York Empire Manufacturing Index. The employment diffusion subindex advanced to its highest level since June 2022 with the average employee workweek climbing over the month too.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
Empire State Manufacturing Survey Exposes A Troubling Disconnect Between Optimism And Reality

The New York Fed’s November survey reveals deteriorating demand beneath a positive headline. Business conditions plunged from 25.5 to 7.8, missing expectations of 18.0. Only 31% reported improvement, 23.2% deterioration and 45.8% no change.

Demand Is Losing Momentum

New orders collapsed from 23.2 to 3.0. Firms reporting rising orders fell from 42.9% to 28.3%, while those reporting declines rose from 19.7% to 25.2%. Another 46.5% saw no change. Declining orders nearly matched rising orders.

Shipments slowed from 13.1 to 8.8, unfilled orders from 14.0 to 10.3 and inventories from 11.6 to 9.2. All remain positive, but incoming demand is weakening faster than ongoing activity. Earlier orders may be sustaining current activity.

Employment Strength Has A Catch

Employment reached 18.1, its highest since June 2022, and the workweek index rose to 13.5. Yet firms adding workers barely increased from 20% to 21.5%. Most improvement came from firms cutting employment falling from 9.8% to 3.4%. Another 75.1% reported unchanged staffing.

That is stronger retention, not a hiring boom. If orders stay weak, hiring freezes and reduced hours may precede layoffs.

Inflation Is Slowing, Not Disappearing

Prices paid fell from 59.5 to 45.9 and prices received from 30.6 to 27.2. The share reporting price declines rounded to zero. Cost inflation moderated, not reversed.

Supply availability remained negative at minus 9.2 and deliveries continued lengthening. During the survey window WTI fell around 9.7% while natural gas rose about 13.8%. Future input price expectations remained at 66.7 versus 41.2 for selling prices, raising pricing power concerns.

The Contradiction Few Are Examining

Future business expectations rose from 21.0 to 28.9 and capital spending intentions to 23.0, their highest since December 2022.

Yet firms expecting higher future shipments fell from 50.4% to 41.4%, those anticipating more hiring declined from 34.5% to 27.4%, and expected unfilled orders dropped from 14.0 to 2.3. Even the share expecting higher new orders declined from 46.6% to 45.2%.

The optimism reflects fewer pessimists more than stronger demand.

Businesses invest not only to expand production but also to survive deteriorating conditions. Automation, energy efficient machinery and equipment that reduces labor costs can raise capital spending even as future hiring and demand weaken.

My strongest suspicion is that some investment plans are defensive, not expansionary. The survey does not identify their purpose, but portraying higher capex intentions as proof of stronger demand while fewer firms anticipate more shipments and hiring is misleading.

The Broader Reality

October ISM manufacturing remained expansionary at 55.5 and manufacturing payrolls added 19,000 jobs, although hours were flat. Philadelphia and Dallas also reported sharp order slowdowns, while tighter small business credit threatens investment.

The Bottom Line

Businesses may be investing to protect profitability and reduce future labor needs while incoming orders weaken. Such investment can support GDP without generating a durable expansion in employment or output.

This is not proof of a manufacturing recession. It is a fragile expansion whose current employment and shipments could become lagging indicators if orders fail to recover. Greater optimism should not be confused with greater economic strength.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
Two different things are getting mashed together here.

Jane’s $4M isn’t money. It’s the price of her shares. The only new cash in the deal is the investors’ $1M, and that came from their existing bank accounts. If the app fails her shares go to zero and not a single dollar disappears, because no dollars were ever created. A price isn’t money. Your house has an appraised value too. Nobody thinks the appraiser printed money.

The startup is production, just like the house. The $1M paid people to build something, and the $2B valuation only exists because customers use the product and save money. It’s the market’s price on real output.

You’re right that if she borrows against those shares, the bank creates new money. But that’s the same thing that happens when anyone takes out a mortgage. It’s a loan that has to be paid back with interest, and the money is destroyed when it’s repaid. If you want to complain that rich people can borrow against stock to avoid capital gains taxes, that’s a fair tax policy argument. But it’s a different argument from “valuations are printing money.”

posts.name: Diane Swonk
posts.text:
Important research on how oil shocks have shifted post pandemic and reinforces longer tail effects of oil shocks and less “look through” dynamics of oil-related price surge than pre-pandemic.

The research is from the Federal Reserve Board economist and highlights the shift to more hawkish stance.  There is uncertainty in that shocks post pandemic have been more persistent.  Is it oil or everything all at once?

It is important because it suggests that the Fed may be more hemmed in to act in response to a series of shocks than in the past. 

That would not be good as it could limit the Fed’s ability to counter an economic downturn if that does not derail inflation for the Fed. 

Fiscal space is limited as well. Even import prices are surging - that is prior to tariff effects. Note many inputs into AI have tariff waivers. The shear surge in demand for AI build out and compute power is pushing up prices on imports at home and abroad. The steel industry is getting premiums from hyperscalers to get orders filled first, further pushing up input costs and making other structures harder to build. That is in addition to the skilled trades people that have been secured to do data center construction. Their wages in the top 12 data center states have gone up 80% faster per year over last four before sweeteners. Other builders can compete and the number of winners of those wage gains is limited. 

All this is to say - inflation is persistent. Good news on lower oil prices is welcome. However, refining capacity still limited and tail of earlier effects are long. 

After (if?) conflict resolved in Middle East, there is more room for downward pressure on oil price. Offsetting some of that downswing will be replenishing of inventories, which have already reached a record low ex China. Those efforts to replenish liquidated oil inventories, limited refining capacity & any rebound in demand in areas hit hardest in emerging Asia will create a floor under energy costs for a bit and elongate tail effects of higher prices. 

Bottom line: Inflation is sticky - demand destruction could but may not fully derail.

quoted.text:
Two labs are pulling away at the AI frontier & one of them goes public this week. The IPO concentrates the industry further, with public market capital and pressure behind it

Concentration is what a lot of people in AI are worried about because:

1) Whoever trains the model decides how it behaves, 
what it will answer, what it treats as true. How it handles questions about health/money/government. Those choices get baked in during training and are hard to undo once the model is widely used.

2) Two suppliers the set the price and the terms. Startups, hospitals, and entire countries end up renting intelligence on someone else’s conditions. Raise prices, change the rules, or restrict access.... everyone downstream has limited options and high switching costs.

3) Concentration is a security risk. When OpenAI agents went rogue and hacked Hugging Face, the closed frontier models (GPT and Claude) refused to help analyze the attack because of their safety guardrails. HF had to use an open weight model they could run themselves to defend their own systems. When the models that control the defaults also control what you’re allowed to do in a crisis, youre dependent on someone else’s rules

FUD

He stated 3 scenarios, let’s not pretend he was just dooming.  

In remarks prepared for a San Francisco Fed symposium on Nov. 16, 2026, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh (and Fed staff modeling) outlined three illustrative AI/“superintelligence” scenarios—not forecasts:
1.  Best case: AI raises productivity, with gains shared broadly between labor and capital. Real GDP growth stays persistently above its long-run average and the economy remains near full employment.
2.  Labor displacement: Automation competes with rather than complements workers, pushing unemployment above levels consistent with full employment.
3.  Disappointment: After heavy capital investment and stock-market gains, expected returns fall, equity valuations drop, the economy slows, and unemployment rises more notably. The economy eventually recovers, but without the anticipated productivity gains.

FED CHAIR WARSH WARNS AI COULD TRIGGER MAJOR ECONOMIC DISRUPTION

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh says emerging technologies, including superintelligence, could fundamentally reshape the economy and monetary policy.

Warsh outlined potential outcomes ranging from broad productivity gains to high unemployment and economic slowdowns if AI fails to meet expectations and equity valuations decline.

He warned that the technology's risks could be highly disruptive and economically costly, while stressing that humans must retain decision-making authority.

The Fed must assess the scale, timing and economic implications of technological change.

posts.name: Michael Pettis
posts.text:
Caixin: "China’s fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% year on year in the first 10 months of the year, a sharper decline than economists expected, suggesting the impact of investment-support measures introduced since August has yet to fully materialize. Manufacturing investment fell 2.9%, while infrastructure investment dropped 5.1%, as a shortage of eligible local projects and limited local government funding continued to constrain infrastructure spending. Private investment also weakened, falling 11.4% in the first 10 months."

What often isn't sufficiently well understood is that a rising trade surplus is the obverse of declining investment. As the gap between production and consumption continues to rise, it logically has to be balanced either by higher domestic investment or by higher net exports.

If it isn't, and because it is proving almost impossible  to get consumption growth to accelerate, China would otherwise be forced to rebalance with a decline in production, along with rising unemployment, something its already-high unemployment levels cannot allow.

Given the increasing difficult in finding productive investment projects, along with rising concerns about the country's rapidly-rising debt burden, it therefore shouldn't surprise anyone that China is locked into ever-rising trade surpluses.
https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-11-16/chinas-fixed-asset-investment-decline-deepens-102505237.html

posts.name: Ted Zhang
posts.text:
Druckenmiller: Watch the Leading Industries, and Ask What Could Go Right Too

My macro approach to the economy has always been looking at businesses as opposed to statistics like unemployment figures or all the stuff that the PhDs look at. So if you've got a business like housing that leads, or retail that's coincident, or trucking that leads, I have found that if you get into management, and even one level down from top management, and you talk about the trends, and if all those leading industries are really, really strong, the economy is probably about to turn up and do very well. And vice versa. If housing is weakening and trucking is weakening, usually the economy is not going to have a good future.

My first boss, Drelles: what's obvious is obviously wrong, and it's already reflected in security prices. This kind of goes back to the invest in the present. If everything is rosy, it's already in the stock price and already in the market. There's nobody left to buy. So you have to constantly be evaluating what could go wrong, but I'll turn that on its head. You also have to evaluate what could go right.

And it's not an accident that almost every stock market bottom happens during a recession and during lousy earnings, and every top happens with consumer confidence high, not low. The world changes, and you're only going to pick up change if you're opening your mind up to how things could be different, whether it's better or worse.

posts.name: Bob McNally
posts.text:
For almost ten years now, and certainly after IEA censored CPS in 2020, I think "peak" demand describes a widely propagated and deeply held narrative with associated curve slopes.

The narrative holds that climate-policy-inspired EV subsidies and mandates will quickly and sufficiently induce a decoupling of road fuel demand from GDP to offset petchem and jet growth, so total liquids demand stops rising around the end of the decade.    This decade, so the narrative went: OECD falls, Non-OECD slows, total growth peaks.

Market data, policy, and geopolitical developments are undermining the credibility of the peak-demand narrative and will eventually do so for China.  Meanwhile, macro weakness, price spikes, and disruptions are hammering demand, lending it temporary validation.

@RapidanEnergy's base-case CAGR for 2030-2050 total liquids demand growth is 0.7%.  We model faster and slower EV adoption scenarios, but in none does total liquids demand peak by 2050.

We agree electrification is cutting into fuel demand, but just not as fast as hoped, advertized, and needed to stop total liquids demand growth.

posts.name: Deepak Shenoy
posts.text:
Current account deficit for the first half of FY27 is about $25bn, with about $7bn deficit in Sep. 

For Sep, Remittances ($11bn) and Services (mostly IT, $19bn) make up for the goods deficit ($30bn). The difference of 7bn is in "income" - mostly dividends/royalties paid. 

For the half year, we saw $125bn come in through "Banking capital" ie NRI deposits from FCNR. ECB by India was about $40bn, which is probably Indian banks lending to NRIs (not dead sure of this but still) This means about 67bn has been added to reserves this far. 

We are probably on track for less than $50bn this year in the CAD. The last quarter (Jan-Mar) is usually a surplus.

Ukraine hit 2 oil depots in Azov in Russia’s Rostov region, the country’s Special Forces command says on Telegram.

Targeted facilities include:
Distribution terminal Transit-Express which is a used to receive, store and dispatch petroleum products
Azovskaya oil depot near the city’s port, with storage capacity of 30,000 cubic meters of petroleum       products
Ukrainian military says both facilities supply petroleum products from Russia to occupied areas of southern Ukraine (Bloomberg)

posts.name: Javier Blas
posts.text:
MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: With data for the first 10 days of November, we can see two trends emerging on Persian Gulf oil exports (ex Iran): 

A) After a very strong start of the month, crude oil flows are now materially lower, running about ~2.0m b/d below than full-month October (equal to 85% of pre-war levels, from 100% in October). The drop is widespread, but particularly acute for Kuwaiti flows. 

B) At the same time, exports of petroleum refined products are significantly higher than in Sep and Oct, suggesting a deliberate effort to prioritize them at the expense of crude. Kuwait and UAE are mostly behind the boost of refined products. All said, Nov 1-10 refined petroleum products exports are running at ~65% of prewar levels, up from 50%-40% in Oct-Sep.

But all together, and ex-Iran Middle East total oil flows are lower than Oct, but roughly on par with September. The composition has changed, however, with crude materially lower, and refined products materially higher.
